Running over = additional injury phase (often causes degloving, crush injuries, tire marks). Incorrect: (A) Sequence is reversed; (C) Ground impact is last; (D) Running over is not the first event in a typical pedestrian strike. Exam pearl: Bumper fracture height = vehicle identification. Waddell's triad = classic pediatric pedestrian injury. Tramline bruising = rod/cylindrical impact. 'Thrown distance' = correlates with vehicle speed.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 23-year-old medical student is brought to the emergency with extreme agitation, paranoid delusions, hyperthermia (temperature 40.2°C), hypertension (BP 185/110 mmHg), tachycardia (HR 155/min), and diaphoresis. He has dilated pupils and is grinding his teeth. His friends say he took 'something at a party.' Urine toxicology is positive for sympathomimetics. Which substance is MOST likely responsible?

options.A: MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine / Ecstasy)
options.B: Heroin
options.C: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)
options.D: Ketamine

questions.explanation: Correct (A): MDMA (Ecstasy/Molly) = serotonin-norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent (primarily serotonergic + sympathomimetic). Features: (1) Sympathomimetic: Hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, mydriasis; (2) Serotonergic: Agitation, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, clonus (trismus/bruxism - jaw clenching = characteristic); (3) Entactogenic: Empathy, euphoria; (4) Life-threatening complications: Serotonin syndrome, hyperthermia (>40°C = brain damage risk), rhabdomyolysis, hyponatremia (SIADH + excess water intake). Key distinguishing features: Bruxism (teeth grinding) + MDMA party + sympathomimetic toxidrome = MDMA. Urine tox: Positive for sympathomimetics (cross-reacts with amphetamines). Treatment: Benzodiazepines (first-line for agitation), cooling, cyproheptadine (serotonin antagonist). Incorrect: (B) Heroin = opioid toxidrome (miosis, respiratory depression, sedation) - opposite of this presentation; (C) GHB = CNS depressant, sedation/coma ('date rape drug'); (D) Ketamine = dissociative, catalepsy, emergence reactions - not primarily sympathomimetic. Exam pearl: MDMA = bruxism + serotonin syndrome + hyponatremia triad. Most dangerous immediate complications: hyperthermia and hyponatremia. BZD = cornerstone of management.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A court orders exhumation of a body for forensic examination 6 months after burial. The magistrate and police are present. During exhumation, which specimen is MOST RELIABLE for toxicological analysis to detect chronic metallic poison exposure (e.g., arsenic) when blood, urine, and soft tissues are decomposed?

options.A: Decomposed liver tissue
options.B: Hair, nail clippings, and bone (especially cortical bone)
options.C: Gastric contents
options.D: Vitreous humor

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Exhumation toxicology - specimen selection when body is decomposed: (1) HAIR: Most valuable for chronic metal poisoning (arsenic, lead, mercury, thallium); Grows 1 cm/month → segmental analysis gives timeline; Arsenic binds to keratin (cysteine sulfur bonds) → persists even after decomposition; (2) NAILS: Similar to hair; keratin-rich; persist long after burial; (3) BONE (cortical): Long-lived; lead accumulates in hydroxyapatite of bone (skeleton stores 95% of body's lead); bone analysis can detect metal poisoning decades later; Cortical bone (femur mid-shaft) preferred over trabecular (more metabolically active → faster turnover). (4) DECOMPOSED LIVER: Some metals may be present but decomposition and soil contamination reduce reliability; (5) VITREOUS HUMOR: Excellent for electrolytes, glucose, some drugs (protected by eye); but less useful for metallic poisons specifically. (6) SOIL SAMPLES: Must be taken for comparison (rule out soil contamination as source of metals). Incorrect: (A) Decomposed liver is less reliable than hair/nail/bone; (C) Gastric contents - largely decomposed at 6 months; (D) Vitreous - valuable for some analyses but less specific for metallic poisoning timeline. Exam pearl: Exhumation toxicology → hair + nail + bone = best. Arsenic = hair/nail (keratin binding). Lead = bone (hydroxyapatite). Always take soil samples for comparison.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with anxiety disorder is found unresponsive after taking multiple diazepam tablets. He has GCS 8, RR 12/min, BP 110/70 mmHg, and normal-sized pupils. He responds to sternal rub. What is the SPECIFIC antidote and its mechanism?

options.A: Naloxone; blocks opioid receptors
options.B: Flumazenil; competitive antagonist at GABA-A benzodiazepine binding site
options.C: N-acetylcysteine; replenishes glutathione
options.D: Physostigmine; inhibits cholinesterase to reverse anticholinergic effects

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Benzodiazepine mechanism: BZD bind to GABA-A receptor at the BZD binding site (between alpha and gamma subunits) → increase FREQUENCY of chloride channel opening → enhanced GABA inhibitory effect → CNS depression. Clinical features of BZD overdose: Sedation, CNS depression, respiratory depression (mild), normal or slightly small pupils (mild miosis), relatively preserved blood pressure. BZD overdose is RARELY fatal in isolation (respiratory depression is mild vs opioids). Antidote: Flumazenil = competitive antagonist at GABA-A BZD binding site → displaces BZD → reverses sedation. CAUTION: (1) Short acting (30-60 min) → re-sedation when effect wears off; (2) CONTRAINDICATED in: BZD-dependent patients (precipitates severe withdrawal/seizures); Mixed overdose with TCAs (may unmask seizure threshold); Raised intracranial pressure. Incorrect: (A) Naloxone = opioid receptor antagonist (pupils would be pinpoint in opioid OD); (C) NAC = paracetamol antidote; (D) Physostigmine = anticholinergic antidote (pupils would be dilated in anticholinergic OD). Exam pearl: BZD overdose alone = mild respiratory depression + NOT life-threatening + normal pupils. Flumazenil = caution in BZD-dependent patients. Always check for mixed overdose.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A severely burnt woman in the ICU makes a statement naming her husband as having set her on fire. She is conscious, oriented, and aware of her impending death. A police officer records the statement. She dies 2 hours later. Subsequently, her husband's defense lawyer argues the dying declaration is inadmissible because: (1) it was not recorded by a Magistrate, and (2) the patient was on morphine for pain, which affected her mental state. Evaluate the legal validity of the dying declaration.

options.A: The declaration is invalid as it must be recorded by a Judicial Magistrate to be admissible in court
options.B: The declaration is valid; a dying declaration can be recorded by any person including a police officer or doctor; opioid use requires case-by-case assessment of mental clarity
options.C: The declaration is invalid because the patient was under the influence of opioids
options.D: A dying declaration requires the patient to be a Hindu to be admissible under Section 32, Indian Evidence Act

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Dying Declaration under Section 32(1) of Indian Evidence Act, 1872: A statement made by a person who has died or is 'expected to die' regarding the circumstances of their death or the cause of death. Key legal principles: (1) CAN be recorded by: Magistrate (preferred), Police officer, Doctor (especially when death is imminent and Magistrate not available), or any private person (even another patient/nurse). (2) Magistrate recording = preferred but NOT mandatory; other recordings ARE admissible; (3) NOT necessary to be on oath; (4) The declarant must be: Conscious, Oriented, Mentally fit to make a coherent statement; (5) Corroboration is not mandatory (can be sole basis for conviction - landmark SC cases); (6) Opioid use: Must assess mental clarity at the TIME of the declaration; if conscious and coherent despite analgesia, the declaration is valid - medical certificate of fitness of mind from the treating doctor strengthens admissibility; (7) Religion, age, gender = irrelevant. Incorrect: (A) Magistrate is preferred, not mandatory; (C) Opioid use alone does not invalidate - depends on actual mental state; (D) No religious restriction in law. Exam pearl: Dying declaration = 'nemo moriturus praesumitur mentiri' (a person about to die is presumed not to lie). Doctor's fitness certificate = critical accompaniment to strengthen dying declaration.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child is brought to the pediatric emergency after ingesting ferrous sulfate tablets from the kitchen cabinet. He is vomiting blood (hematemesis) and has bloody diarrhea. Initial serum iron is 620 mcg/dL (normal 60-160 mcg/dL). He appears lethargic. Which is the CORRECT chelating agent and the STAGE of iron poisoning?

options.A: EDTA; Stage I (GI phase)
options.B: Deferoxamine; Stage II (relative recovery), but treatment indicated due to serious toxicity
options.C: Deferoxamine; Stage I (GI phase) - this level indicates serious systemic toxicity
options.D: Dimercaprol (BAL); Stage III (systemic toxicity)

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Iron poisoning stages: Stage I (0-6 hours) = GI phase: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, GI hemorrhage (direct mucosal toxicity); Stage II (6-24 hours) = Apparent recovery/quiet phase (misleading - toxin absorbed, less GI symptoms but systemic injury ongoing); Stage III (12-48 hours) = Systemic toxicity: Shock, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, liver failure; Stage IV = Hepatic failure (2-5 days); Stage V = Pyloric/GI scarring (strictures, 2-6 weeks). Serum iron interpretation: >350 mcg/dL = systemic toxicity likely; >500 mcg/dL = serious toxicity (this child has 620 = serious). This child is in Stage I (GI bleeding) but with very high iron level = systemic toxicity imminent/present. Chelating agent: Deferoxamine (Desferrioxamine): Chelates free iron → ferrioxamine (complex) → excreted in urine (turns orange/vin rosé color = sign of treatment); Given IV in serious toxicity (IM in milder cases). Incorrect: (A) EDTA is not used for iron; (B) Stage II is the 'quiet phase' - not what this child has (active GI bleeding); (D) BAL/Dimercaprol is for arsenic, lead, mercury. Exam pearl: Deferoxamine = iron chelation. Vin rosé urine = confirms iron-ferrioxamine excretion. Serum iron >500 = deferoxamine regardless of stage. GI symptoms ± high iron level = Stage I, treat aggressively.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 16-year-old rape survivor presents at 19 weeks of gestation. She wants to terminate the pregnancy but her parents refuse. Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 (India), what is the CORRECT legal position?

options.A: Termination is not possible as gestational age exceeds 18 weeks for minors
options.B: Termination can be done up to 20 weeks with one doctor's opinion; survivor's consent (not parental consent) is sufficient as she is the pregnant woman; guardian consent also noted for minor
options.C: Parental refusal legally blocks the procedure regardless of gestational age
options.D: A court order is mandatory for all rape survivors seeking termination beyond 12 weeks

questions.explanation: Correct (B): MTP Amendment Act 2021 (India) - key provisions: Gestational limits: (1) Up to 20 weeks: ONE RMP's opinion required; (2) 20-24 weeks: TWO RMPs' opinion required; Specific categories eligible for 20-24 week termination: Survivors of rape/sexual assault, Minors, Differently-abled women, Mentally ill women, Fetal abnormality detected after 20 weeks; (3) Beyond 24 weeks: Only if fetal abnormality detected - Medical Board approval (State-level board). For this 16-year-old rape survivor at 19 weeks: (1) Gestational age 19 weeks = within 20-week limit; (2) ONE RMP opinion sufficient; (3) For minors, guardian consent is required IN ADDITION TO (not instead of) the pregnant woman's own will (she is the patient); (4) Rape survivor category = additional protection; her personal consent IS legally recognized. Parental refusal: Parents/guardians cannot force continuation against the survivor's wishes; court can be approached if impasse. Incorrect: (A) 20-week limit applies, not 18 weeks; (B) is correct; (C) Parental refusal does not legally override survivor's rights; (D) Court order not mandatory for all rape survivors - only beyond 24 weeks without medical board clearance. Exam pearl: MTP 2021: Up to 20 weeks = 1 RMP; 20-24 weeks = 2 RMPs + specific categories (rape, minors, etc.); >24 weeks = Medical Board + fetal abnormality only.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A family of four presents to the emergency 8 hours after consuming wild mushrooms gathered from a forest. All family members have severe vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. By 24-48 hours, two family members develop acute liver failure with coagulopathy (INR 4.2) and rising bilirubin, despite initial apparent improvement (quiet period). Which mushroom toxin and mechanism is MOST likely responsible?

options.A: Muscarine; inhibits acetylcholinesterase causing cholinergic crisis
options.B: Amatoxin (alpha-amanitin) from Amanita phalloides; inhibits RNA polymerase II causing delayed hepatotoxicity
options.C: Ibotenic acid/Muscimol; GABA-A and glutamate receptor modulation
options.D: Psilocybin; serotonin-like effects causing hallucinations

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Amanita phalloides ('Death Cap') poisoning - MOST lethal mushroom poisoning worldwide. Toxin: Amatoxins (alpha-amanitin) + Phallotoxins. Mechanism: Amatoxin inhibits RNA polymerase II (responsible for transcription of mRNA in eukaryotes) → protein synthesis halted → cell death → hepatocellular necrosis (primarily) + renal tubular injury. Clinical phases: Phase 1 (6-24 hours): GI symptoms - vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain; Phase 2 (24-48 hours): Apparent clinical improvement/quiet phase (DECEPTIVE - actually allows toxin to concentrate in liver); Phase 3 (48-72 hours): Acute liver failure - jaundice, coagulopathy, hepatic encephalopathy; Phase 4: Death or recovery (with liver transplant). Treatment: No specific antidote; Silibinin (milk thistle extract) + N-acetylcysteine + liver transplant if ALF. Incorrect: (A) Muscarine causes cholinergic symptoms (DUMBELS) - EARLY onset (30-90 min); (C) Ibotenic acid = CNS symptoms (delirium, ataxia) - EARLY; (D) Psilocybin = hallucinogenic (no liver failure). Exam pearl: Delayed-onset liver failure after mushroom ingestion = Amanita phalloides until proven otherwise. 'Quiet period' = classic trap (patient and doctor falsely reassured). Amatoxin = RNA Pol II inhibitor = protein synthesis failure.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old electrician is found at a worksite with an electrical burn. He has a small, charred entry wound on the palm of his right hand with a dry, leathery, pale center (Joule burns/electrothermal mark). On the other hand, there is a larger, irregular exit wound. The ECG shows ventricular fibrillation. Which statement about electrical injuries is MOST accurate?

options.A: High voltage (>1000 V) injuries typically show smaller wounds than low voltage injuries
options.B: Entry wounds are typically larger than exit wounds in electrical injuries
options.C: The entry wound (electrothermal/Joule burn) shows a characteristic dry, pale, depressed center with raised edges; exit wounds are larger; ventricular fibrillation is the most common cause of death in AC electrocution
options.D: DC (direct current) is more likely to cause ventricular fibrillation than AC at the same voltage

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Electrical injury characteristics: Entry wound (Electrothermal mark/Joule burn): (1) Typically SMALLER; (2) Dry, leathery, pale/white/gray central depressed area (coagulative necrosis); (3) Raised, hyperemic edges; (4) Circular/oval; (5) Location: Where current enters body (hand touching wire). Exit wound: (1) Larger, irregular, more destructive; (2) Where current grounds out (foot to ground usually); (3) More extensive tissue damage. Cause of death in electrocution: (1) AC (Alternating Current) = MORE DANGEROUS for cardiac arrhythmias; (2) AC at 50-60 Hz (household current) = exactly the range causing ventricular fibrillation (cardiac vulnerable period stimulation); (3) VF = most common cause of death in low-voltage AC electrocution; (4) High voltage (>1000 V) = cardiac standstill + burns + respiratory center paralysis. DC (Direct Current): Causes sustained muscle spasm (cannot let go), respiratory muscle contraction, but LESS likely to cause VF than AC. Incorrect: (A) High voltage = more extensive burns; (B) Entry < exit wound (opposite); (D) AC is more dangerous for VF, not DC. Exam pearl: AC (50-60 Hz) = VF = most dangerous. DC = sustained tetanic contraction. Entry wound = small/pale/dry. Exit wound = large/ragged.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old man collapses and dies suddenly while playing cricket. At autopsy, the pathologist finds significant coronary artery disease (LAD 80% stenosis). The heart shows no acute myocardial infarction histologically. There are no external injuries, toxicology is negative. The family requests that the death be certified as natural. Which is the MOST accurate cause of death and medico-legal classification?

options.A: Sudden cardiac death due to coronary artery disease; natural death; no inquest required
options.B: The death is unclassified as no myocardial infarction was found; further investigation required
options.C: Sudden cardiac death due to coronary artery disease; natural death; inquest may still be required as it was an unwitnessed sudden death in the community
options.D: Physical exertion during cricket contributed to death, making this an accidental death

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Sudden Cardiac Death (SCD): Definition: Unexpected death from cardiac cause within 1 hour of symptom onset (or within 24 hours if unwitnessed). Mechanism: Significant CAD (≥75% stenosis of a major vessel) → electrical instability → VF → cardiac arrest. NOTE: Acute MI takes 4-6 hours to show histological changes; death in VF occurs before histological infarction can develop. Therefore: NO HISTOLOGICAL MI does NOT exclude cardiac death from CAD. Classification: Medico-legal: SCD from CAD = NATURAL DEATH. However, in India (and internationally), sudden unexpected deaths in the community require: (1) Police intimation (as per CrPC Section 174 - inquest in cases of sudden/unnatural/suspicious deaths); (2) Autopsy to establish cause; (3) Exclusion of unnatural causes. After completing autopsy establishing natural cause = certified as natural death. Incorrect: (A) Inquest is still mandated even for natural sudden deaths (to exclude foul play); (B) SCD can occur without histological MI (VF from ischemia); (D) Physical exertion is a trigger but the underlying cause is still the CAD - it remains natural death. Exam pearl: Sudden death + no histological MI + significant CAD = SCD from CAD = natural death. Histological changes of MI: Earliest changes at 4-6 hours (wavy fibers), obvious at 12-24 hours (coagulative necrosis).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man presents 30 minutes after consuming a herbal remedy. He has: tingling and numbness of lips, tongue, and fingertips (paraesthesias), followed by severe chest pain, hypotension (BP 70/40 mmHg), bradycardia (HR 38/min) with ECG showing complete heart block, and weakness of all limbs. He reports a feeling of 'heat all over.' Toxicology later confirms aconitine. What is the mechanism and the MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Nicotinic ACh receptor blockade; neostigmine
options.B: Voltage-gated sodium channel activation (keeping channels open); supportive care + atropine for bradycardia + amiodarone for refractory arrhythmias + cardiopulmonary bypass if needed
options.C: Potassium channel blockade causing prolonged repolarization; magnesium sulfate
options.D: Calcium channel blockade; calcium gluconate IV

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Aconitine (from Aconitum napellus - Monkshood/Wolfsbane/Bachnaag/Vatsnabh): One of the most toxic plant alkaloids. Mechanism: Binds to and PERMANENTLY ACTIVATES voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) → keeps Na channels open → persistent membrane depolarization → initial activation (tingling, burning) → then INACTIVATION (weakness, paralysis). Also activates cardiac Nav channels → severe bradycardia, heart block, arrhythmias, hypotension. Clinical features: (1) Initial: Burning/tingling of mouth, lips, skin (activated Nav channels causing paresthesias); (2) GI: Nausea, vomiting; (3) Cardiovascular: Bradycardia, heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension; (4) Neuromuscular: Weakness, paralysis, respiratory failure. Treatment: NO specific antidote: (1) Supportive care; (2) Atropine for bradycardia; (3) Antiarrhythmics (amiodarone/lidocaine for ventricular arrhythmias); (4) Cardiopulmonary bypass (ECMO) in refractory cases as a bridge; (5) Activated charcoal if early presentation. Incorrect: (A) Not nicotinic; neostigmine inappropriate; (C) Aconitine activates (not blocks) sodium channels; (D) Calcium gluconate = calcium channel blocker reversal, not applicable. Exam pearl: Aconitine = Nav channel ACTIVATOR (keeps open) → tingling → heart block. Vatsnabh/bachnaag = traditional Ayurvedic poison. No antidote; ECMO may be lifesaving. Differentiate from VGNa BLOCKERS (local anesthetics, TCAs).
